blocks.md: The decennial **US Census** asked a long-form questionnaire of a sample of households (about one in six) through 2000; public-use microdata samples cover 1–5% of the population. From 2005 the long form was replaced by the **American Community Survey (ACS)**, an annual survey of about 1% of households, often pooled over three or five years. **IPUMS** (University of Minnesota) distributes both with consistent variable codes.

- Country of birth and citizenship, so immigrants can be identified (born abroad, whether naturalized or not)
- Education, age (hence potential experience), occupation, industry and location (state, metropolitan area, county groups that map to commuting zones)
- Prior-year earnings, weeks worked and usual hours, so annual and weekly earnings and hours can be built

| Strength | Weakness |
| --- | --- |
| Very large samples: fine cells by education × experience, or by occupation × region | Only every ten years before 2005 |
| Birthplace and citizenship for every person | Earnings are top-coded ([Top Coding](note:top-coding)) and self-reported |
| Consistent coding across decades via IPUMS | Occupation and geography codes change over time and need crosswalks |

- Borjas (2003) builds 160 education × experience × census-year cells from the 1960–1990 Censuses (and pooled March CPS files for 2000).
- Burstein, Hanson, Tian and Vogel (2020) use the 1980 Census and the 2012 three-year ACS to measure changes in native and immigrant employment by commuting zone and occupation.
